Loan Comparison Calculator

To compare loans, look at the total cost of borrowing (all interest plus fees), not just the rate or the monthly payment. Enter each offer's amount, rate, term and fees: for 20,000 over 5 years, a 5.9% loan with a 500 fee costs 3,643.60 in total, slightly less than a 6.9% loan with no fee at 3,704.86.

Loan offers

Fees are one-off costs such as an arrangement or origination fee. If a fee is added to the loan instead of paid up front, add it to the amount.

Everything runs in your browser. Nothing you type is sent anywhere.

Three numbers to compare

  • Monthly payment (EMI): what you pay each month. It needs to fit your budget comfortably.
  • Total interest: what the lender charges for the money, over the whole term.
  • Total cost of borrowing: interest plus fees. This is the fairest way to compare offers, and the calculator picks the cheapest loan by this number.

Worked example

Three offers for 20,000:

OfferMonthlyInterestFeeTotal cost
A: 6.9%, 5 years395.083,704.8603,704.86
B: 5.9%, 5 years385.733,143.605003,643.60
C: 6.9%, 3 years616.632,198.6102,198.61

Offer B has a lower rate than A, but its 500 fee eats most of the saving: it's only 61.26 cheaper. Offer C has the same rate as A but costs about 1,506 less, simply because you borrow for two fewer years. The catch is a monthly payment 221.55 higher. If you can afford it, the shorter term is the biggest saving here.

The formula

Monthly payment = P × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)^−n) Total interest = monthly payment × n − P Total cost = total interest + fees P = amount, i = yearly rate ÷ 1,200, n = months

APR and fees

The APR (annual percentage rate) includes fees as well as interest, so it's meant to make offers comparable. When you add a fee, the calculator estimates the APR: the rate you'd effectively pay if you received the amount minus the fee and repaid the same monthly payments. Lenders' official APRs can differ a little because of rules about which fees count and how days are counted.

Watch for fees that are added to the loan rather than paid up front. Then you pay interest on the fee too: add it to the amount instead of the fees box.

Other things to check before choosing

  • Early repayment charges: if you might pay off early, a loan without them is worth more.
  • Fixed or variable rate: a variable rate can rise. This calculator assumes the rate stays the same.
  • Representative rates: advertised rates may only be offered to some applicants. Compare the rate you're actually offered.
  • Insurance and extras: payment protection or other add-ons increase the cost and are usually optional.

For a full repayment schedule of one loan, or to see how overpaying shortens it, use the loan calculator.

Results are estimates for comparison. Your lender's documents show the exact figures.

Frequently asked questions

How do I compare two loans?

Compare the total cost of borrowing: all the interest plus any fees. Enter each offer above and the calculator highlights the cheapest.

Is a lower interest rate always cheaper?

No. A fee can make a lower-rate loan cost more, and a longer term increases total interest even at the same rate.

Is it better to take a shorter loan term?

A shorter term costs less interest in total but has higher monthly payments. Choose the shortest term whose payment you can comfortably afford.

What is APR?

The annual percentage rate includes interest and compulsory fees, expressed as a yearly rate. It is designed to make loan offers easier to compare.

Can I compare car loans and personal loans?

Yes. Any fixed-rate loan with equal monthly payments can be compared, including car, personal, student and home loans.
